title: Tracing a requirements worksheet to its checks

blocks.text: A water utility (a fictional one) keeps its stakeholder-requirements worksheet as data. Each requirement is a dictionary `{"id", "stakeholder", "text"}`. Each automated check that ran on the latest plan is a dictionary `{"name", "covers", "passed"}`, where `covers` lists the requirement ids the check proves. Before the plan goes to the regulator, the team wants the worksheet's status, requirement by requirement and stakeholder by stakeholder.

items: `trace(requirements, checks)`: each requirement id mapped to one of three states. **UNTESTED** when no check covers it; **MET** when at least one check covers it and every check covering it passed; **FAILED** when a check covering it failed.
`by_stakeholder(requirements, status)`: for each stakeholder, how many of their requirements are in each of the three states, with every state present, zero or not.

blocks.text: Before you code, take a requirement covered by two checks, one passed and one failed, and say which state it is in and why the worksheet must not call it met. The tests use small hand-made worksheets. About twenty lines.

cases.says: each requirement is met, failed or untested by the checks that cover it
each stakeholder's requirements are counted by state
one failing check among several fails the requirement
a state no requirement of a stakeholder is in still shows a zero
a check that covers several requirements counts for each of them

origin.section: A Requirements Worksheet Ties Each Need to a Model Feature and a Check

concepts: a worksheet ties each requirement to the checks that prove it and reports met, failed and untested needs
